summary: Describes the Intrusion Detection Exchange Protocol, an application-level protocol for exchanging data between intrusion detection entities. It supports mutual authentication, integrity and confidentiality and carries IDMEF messages. This RFC is experimental.

eli5.summary: This is the delivery truck for alarm reports. IDXP carries them between security systems, checks that both ends are who they claim, and keeps the contents private and untampered.

questions: how do intrusion detection systems exchange alerts
subtitle: A protocol for intrusion detection systems to exchange alerts and analysis over a secure connection.

tldr.problem: Intrusion detection systems and security managers need to exchange structured alert messages and analysis data with mutual authentication, integrity, and confidentiality, often through intermediate proxies.
tldr.mechanism: IDXP is built on top of BEEP, a generic connection framework, and uses BEEP security profiles for authentication and encryption. Peers exchange IDMEF messages and optional text or binary data over BEEP channels.
tldr.outcome: Intrusion detection entities can securely share alerts in a many-to-many relationship with transparent proxying, though deployment depends on BEEP and chosen security profiles.

facts.label: Peer relationships
facts.value: Many-to-many (managers); analyzers only talk to managers

today: RFC 4767 is Experimental and defines the IDXP profile, companion to RFC 4765 (IDMEF), both work from the Intrusion Detection Working Group. IDXP deployment has been limited; more prevalent approaches include direct use of HTTPS/TLS for IDS data exchange or specialized IDS management protocols. The work is preserved as a reference design for IDS communications.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
IDXP, the Intrusion Detection Exchange Protocol, is an application-level protocol for exchanging data between intrusion detection entities. These entities are typically analyzers (which monitor networks or hosts and generate alerts) and managers (which collect, analyze, and act on alerts). IDXP is a BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol) profile, meaning it builds on top of BEEP's connection management, asynchronous message handling, and security framework.

The protocol is designed to carry IDMEF messages (Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format, defined in RFC 4765), which provide a standard structured format for intrusion detection data. IDXP also supports unstructured text and binary data. The protocol handles the security-sensitive nature of intrusion detection exchanges through BEEP's security profiles (such as TLS) for mutual authentication, integrity protection, and confidentiality. It is published as Experimental.
sections.eli5: When security sensors detect attacks, they need to send reports to the central monitoring station and to each other. IDXP is the locked and verified communication channel they use.

sections.title: Connection Model and Data Transfer
sections.content:
IDXP peers form a many-to-many relationship. An analyzer may communicate with multiple managers, and a manager may communicate with multiple analyzers or other managers. Critically, analyzers MUST NOT communicate directly with other analyzers; only managers can act as intermediaries. This hierarchy aids in network organization and aggregation of alerts.

To establish an IDXP exchange, a peer initiates a BEEP session and opens one or more BEEP channels using the IDXP profile. Before any IDXP communication, peers SHOULD negotiate a BEEP security profile (such as TLS) to establish mutual authentication and encrypt the channel. Following successful security negotiation, peers exchange IDXP-Greeting elements to identify themselves and negotiate channel options.

Data is transferred using one or more BEEP channels within a single BEEP session. Each channel operates independently and may be categorized by content type (e.g., network-based alerts on one channel, host-based alerts on another). This multi-channel structure allows peers to prioritize and organize alert traffic. Peers may remain open even while idle, reducing the overhead of repeatedly setting up new sessions and channels.
sections.eli5: Sensors talk to managers, managers talk to managers, but sensors never talk directly to each other. Each conversation is over its own locked and verified channel.

sections.title: Message Elements and Protocol Semantics
sections.content:
IDXP messages are XML documents with a MIME Content-Type of text/xml, text/plain, or application/octet-stream. The protocol defines three main elements. The IDXP-Greeting element, exchanged at channel start, identifies the peer (analyzer or manager) and may contain optional Option sub-elements for channel configuration. The Option element conveys channel parameters such as channelPriority (allowing prioritization of high-severity alerts) or streamType (specifying content types like IDMEF, text, or binary).

The IDMEF-Message element carries structured intrusion detection data. The exact schema is defined in RFC 4765 but is not duplicated here; IDXP simply provides the transport. BEEP's message-oriented design means each BEEP message carries one or more IDXP elements.

Peers send the IDXP-Greeting using BEEP MSG messages. If successful, the listening peer includes a reply element (either ok or error) in its BEEP response. Channel or session closure is performed using BEEP's close mechanism.
sections.eli5: Messages are wrapped in XML and say what kind of data they carry. A greeting says 'I am a sensor' or 'I am the manager', and then alerts flow across the channel in the agreed-upon format.

sections.title: Proxying and Tunneling
sections.content:
IDXP supports transparent proxying for relay and aggregation scenarios. An intermediate proxy may sit between analyzers and managers, forwarding alerts without decryption. Proxies are always considered untrustworthy; trust is placed only in the two end IDXP peers. End-to-end security is established by the peers before data reaches a proxy, so the proxy cannot tamper with encrypted messages.

For scenarios where a chain of proxies is needed (for example, department proxies forwarding to a company-wide manager through a firewall), IDXP supports the BEEP TUNNEL profile as a tuning profile. TUNNEL creates an application-layer tunnel transparently forwarding data over a sequence of proxies. A peer connects to a proxy, negotiates TUNNEL with authentication, the proxy connects to the next hop and negotiates TUNNEL again, and this process continues until the final peer is reached. Once the tunnel is established, the peers establish the BEEP security profile and IDXP profile over the tunnel, achieving end-to-end encryption.
sections.eli5: Proxies can sit in the middle and forward locked boxes without opening them. If you need to go through many routers, TUNNEL lets you build a chain of forwarding without anyone in the middle seeing your data.

sections.title: Security Model and Requirements
sections.content:
IDXP delegates security to underlying BEEP security profiles. A BEEP security profile SHOULD be negotiated before the IDXP profile is used, offering mutual authentication, integrity protection, and confidentiality. The TLS profile is explicitly recommended as meeting these requirements. Profiles based on SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) may also be suitable.

The trust model treats all proxies as untrustworthy. IDXP peers establish security directly with each other, ensuring that proxies cannot read or modify alert data. Only after successful security negotiation are peers considered trustworthy for the IDXP exchange.

Fulfillment of the IDWG communications protocol requirements is addressed: IDXP provides reliable message transmission through BEEP, works with firewalls (optionally via TUNNEL), supports mutual authentication through security profiles, provides message confidentiality and integrity through encryption and MACs, achieves per-source authentication by identifying the source peer, offers denial-of-service awareness (though mitigation is the responsibility of implementations), prevents message duplication through BEEP's message handling, and allows fragmentation and reassembly.

The RFC advises careful selection of BEEP security profiles and proper configuration of the trust model. Without an appropriate security profile, the IDXP conversation is unprotected. Additionally, TUNNEL introduces complexity and should only be used when needed; direct connections are preferred when feasible.
sections.eli5: IDXP itself does not encrypt—it relies on TLS or similar to lock the channel. Proxies cannot read the messages even if they try. Both sides prove who they are before any alerts are sent.
